title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
summary: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at this https URL .

title: DuplexAct: How Interactive Are Frontier Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models?
summary: End-to-end (E2E) full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) enable simutanous listening and speaking continously, requiring models to take appropriate interaction actions as conversations unfold. However, existing benchmarks lack a structured action-level formulation, often evaluate action occurrence rather than success, and provide limited coverage of diverse real-world conversations. We introduce DuplexAct, a benchmark for evaluating interaction action taking in E2E FD-SLMs. DuplexAct defines a three-level action taxonomy spanning eight interaction actions and 24 corresponding interaction conditions. We further characterize successful action-taking through immediate execution and subsequent follow-through, and develop action-specific evaluation metrics for both. DuplexAct contains 4,691 test instances spanning casual conversation, meetings, customer service, and interviews, including 2,531 instances derived from real-world conversational recordings. Together, DuplexAct provides a structured and real-world-grounded framework for systematically assessing how E2E FD-SLMs participate in ongoing spoken interaction.

title: Evidence-First Agentic Verification
summary: Long-horizon, semi-verifiable agentic tasks often rely on rubric-based evaluation, but the evidence needed to assess these tasks can be spread across the environment state and the execution trace. A judge may overlook this evidence or accept unsupported claims, including an agent's own reports of success. When rubric verdicts serve as reinforcement-learning rewards, such errors can reinforce undesirable behavior. We introduce Sauron, an evidence-first agentic verifier that investigates both state and trace and relies on a claim only after independently validating it against its source. Bounded queries and joint investigation of related criteria reduce context use and redundant work, and each verdict carries an auditable receipt of its supporting evidence. Across 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes, Sauron achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers on all eight backbones tested while costing less than Gandalf, the strongest baseline. With GPT-5.6 Sol, it reaches 0.96 F1 versus Gandalf's 0.92 at 23% lower cost, with a wider margin on process criteria. On a paired fault-injection suite covering 13 families, several of which simulate reward hacking, Sauron detects 97% of injected failures while flagging only 2% of clean controls, outperforming baselines even when they are given the full trace. On TRAIL, a benchmark for detecting and localizing real agent errors, Sauron leads both Gandalf and TRAIL's own judge on all three quality metrics.

title: Adaptive-Group Process Rewards for GUI Agents
summary: Training graphical user interface (GUI) agents with reinforcement learning suffers from sparse outcome rewards, leading to inefficient learning. Process rewards offer a promising direction for credit assignment to intermediate actions; however, accurately evaluating an action requires identifying evidence across long-horizon GUI trajectories, as its value may depend on information beyond its immediate state and observation. In this paper, we propose an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group for action correctness and contribution to the subgoal. At the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, and further refines these assessments by leveraging the context of all groups in the trajectory. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation. We further augment GRPO's outcome advantage with the proposed process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
summary: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.

title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training GPU-hours close to GRPO. Further experiments show improved sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and support the meter's ability to distinguish step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes. title: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.

title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
summary: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.

title: Cowork-Gym: Synthesizing Interactive Work Environments at Scale
summary: Cowork agents navigate dependencies across tools and files while adapting to changing user requirements and edits to shared workspaces. Scaling such environments requires maintaining consistency among task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria. We introduce Cowork-Gym, a framework that synthesizes Cowork environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair generated environments. To capture realistic Cowork dynamics, a stateful user simulator responds to the agent's actions through dialogue and direct edits to the shared workspace. We synthesize 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and use them to post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B Qwen models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation. Averaged across six agentic benchmarks, these models outperform their corresponding base checkpoints by 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points, respectively. Ours-27B ranks second overall among the evaluated models and achieves the highest average scores on PawBench and ClawEval, outperforming models with over 100B total parameters on both benchmarks.

title: When Should Enterprise Policy Decisions Be Learned, and When Should They Be Reasoned?
summary: An enterprise agent that answers under a written policy must choose an action before it says anything: answer, ask for a missing fact, ask for confirmation, call one or several tools, escalate, or refuse. Holding one 27B Korean enterprise model fixed, we vary whether the decision is a generated JSON object or a single constrained token, and whether the model may reason first. On 2800 in-distribution items we did not detect an accuracy difference between the two deployed paths (93.46% vs 94.14%), while they differ about tenfold in restart stability (3.00% of actions flip vs 0.29%); they also differ in reasoning, so this is an operational comparison. On a sealed benchmark of 300 items whose labels come from a hidden executable policy, reasoning is worth +17.3 points [+12.3, +23.0] on exact action. With reasoning off, the format difference was 0.0 points [-4.3, +4.0], a failure to detect an advantage for either interface, not equivalence; with reasoning on it is unresolved. Against a token-matched random control, boundary-targeted supervision moves the two covered boundaries by +17.5 and +20.0 points and leaves a held-out boundary unchanged. In a 3-seed training x reasoning factorial, the sealed-rendering interaction is -4.9 [-8.1, -1.7], consistent with partial substitution. All supervision was Korean. On independently rendered English versions, the model is 0.82 points lower [-2.68, +0.93] with reasoning on, the same order as re-rendering in Korean; the reasoning-off gain from targeted supervision is not stable in either language, so we do not claim transfer. The original text stays private as the confirmatory set. An open-model re-rendering made after these results reproduced the reasoning effect and the English verdict; the interaction kept its sign but did not replicate under item-clustered intervals. We release the model and that re-rendering with gold labels.

title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
summary: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in this https URL .

title: Releasing the Inner Jev: A Simple Recipe for Open Decision Models
summary: LLM-based decision-making systems, also called System One models, have recently gained popularity, most notably through Jev (Almeida, 2026). Given a typed input state, a question, and a set of options, they return a probability for each option in a single forward pass, without text generation. We show that existing open instruction-tuned language models can achieve comparable performance \textit{without any additional training}, by reading out answers from letters (A, B, C, etc.) in the model's output logits at the last token position. Furthermore, we show how a simple supervised fine-tuning recipe can improve their performance further. We evaluate four open instruction-tuned language models: Gemma 4 31B, Gemma 4 12B, Qwen3.6-27B, and Qwen3.5-4B. We fine-tune each using LoRA and a decision head initialized from a slice of the language model head. Furthermore, we introduce OpenDecisions, a novel 2,352-question validation dataset designed to reflect the task composition of JevBench (JevBench main- tainers, 2026) and which computes a Capability score based on accuracy and calibration metrics. Without fine-tuning, Gemma 4 31B scores 79.6 on OpenDecisions, compared to Jev's 80.1. After undergoing our fine-tuning recipe, it scores 84.4 on OpenDecisions and 81.5 on JevBench v1.7, outperforming Jev by 4.3 and 4.4 Capability points respectively and setting a new state-of-the-art on OpenDecisions. On a suite of public decision datasets, our models achieve accuracy comparable to Jev, with lower calibration error. Our results show that open language models already possess System One capabilities, and with simple fine-tuning they outperform Jev on a wide range of decision tasks. We release our models, serving code, and OpenDecisions.

title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
summary: Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension. In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements. We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/\delta))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/\delta))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.

title: WildTrace: Evaluating Training Data Detection in Realistic Large-Scale LLM Post-Training
summary: Although post-training significantly enhances model performance, the use of massive undisclosed data raises concerns about benchmark contamination and copyright infringement. This drives growing interest in training data detection for post-trained models. Existing evaluations for training data detection often leverage benchmarks constructed post hoc, which can introduce distribution shifts. Alternatively, controlled evaluations rely on small-scale training setups that diverge from realistic post-training settings. As a result, their reported performance may not faithfully reflect the effectiveness of detection methods in real-world scenarios. To this end, we introduce \textsc{\method}, a reliable benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods in realistic, large-scale post-training settings. Built on a multi-stage pipeline, \method\space encompasses stage-specific models throughout the post-training lifecycle, spanning SFT, DPO, and RL. To perform a reliable evaluation, we construct model-specific evaluation sets across four diverse tasks, featuring distribution-matched members and non-members with verifiable membership labels. Our results reveal that even the best-performing method achieves an average AUC of only 0.529 on our benchmark, which approaches random-guessing level (0.5). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluation protocols can significantly affect measured detection performance. These findings highlight the significant potential for developing effective, practical, and robust detection methods under realistic scenarios.

title: The Format is the Filter: Scoring Format Fixes What an LLM Judge Can Express
summary: When an LLM judge filters instruction-tuning data, its scoring format (binary verdict, 1--5 rating, 0--100 score, or comparison) is rarely justified or ablated. Holding the candidate pool, judge prompt, decoding and selection budget fixed, we score 15,406 UltraFeedback candidates under five formats with three judges, curate, fine-tune 66 models, and evaluate them with four judges. A 0--100 scale is worth only 7--12 equally used levels, two to three times a 1--5 scale rather than twenty, and a binary verdict leaves the top score tied in 77--78\% of prompts, so most selections are made at random. These properties are set by the format almost independently of the judge. Kendall's $\tau_b$ hides them: it ranks binary best while $\tau_a$ and top-1 agreement rank it last, because it discounts the ties a selector must break at random. Both comparative formats inherit a slot bias whose sign differs across judges. Downstream, curated data beat random selection under every evaluation judge, robust to length and markdown adjustment, but no ordering among formats is detectable. We propose four quantities that judge-based curation pipelines should report.

title: SFT Leaves a Reproducible Signature in Activation Geometry: Calibrating Post-Training Interpretability Against Run-to-Run Noise
summary: A model diff credits post-training with whatever separates a base checkpoint from one post-trained descendant, presuming a rerun would land close by. On the sparse co-activation graph of Qwen3-1.7B it does not: two LoRA-SFT reruns sit over half as far apart as either sits from the base. We score each base-to-post contrast against the run-to-run band of its own recipe, and show that $k$ runs certify no better than $p=1/(k+1)$ under run exchangeability, however large the effect, so the band $z$-score is a descriptive scale. SFT leaves a large, reproducible signature: base $\to$ SFT displaces the graph by 17.8 pairwise-distance SDs beyond the mean distance between four independent LoRA-SFT runs, and the pre-registered estimator replicates on Llama-3.1-8B with Llama-Scope. At 29 steps each, four SFT and four DPO runs occupy disjoint displacement ranges, a gap $5.0\times$ and $5.6\times$ the spreads of the two arms, without any band. All bands use graphs built on one GPU architecture. Three other readings stop short of a verdict: DPO band counts (3/4, 1/4, 3/4 contrasts outside at 12, 29, 60 steps) show no consistent dose ordering while its displacement stays flat; light GRPO is a secondary non-detection, not an absence, and we run no equivalence test; and the graph concentration read as an RL signature is already in the zero-RL base. A pre-registered causal sweep at three edge budgets on 4,816 held-out prompts found the displaced sources load-bearing ($12\times$ a matched random control in mean, $3.5\times$ in median at 10,000 edges), but their stage-specificity interaction reversed at two budgets and the third failed its faithfulness gate, so we claim calibrated structural displacement, not a changed mechanism. Scope: one backbone, one SFT recipe and general-text probe states for the full protocol.

title: VL-DocIR: A Benchmark for Vision-Based Long Document Information Retrieval
summary: Vision-based document retrieval has improved rapidly, but current evaluation settings still emphasize short documents and single relevant pages. This leaves an important gap between leaderboard performance and realistic long-document retrieval, where the evidence needed to answer a query may span multiple pages or even multiple documents. We present VL-DocIR, a page-level benchmark for evidence-complete visual long-document retrieval. VL-DocIR is built from 29,641 HTML-born documents rendered into 388,548 page images from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements. It contains 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures, covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document evidence configurations. Evidence annotations are grounded to rendered pages and HTML element identifiers, and queries are filtered with a cleaning pipeline targeting clarity, correctness, closedness, and the absence of explicit layout references. We evaluate leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers together with diagnostic retrieval settings such as document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles. The strongest evaluated configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10 under structure-balanced Macro evaluation, but source- and evidence-structure breakdowns show that cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and that document-context scoring is especially helpful for within-document multi-page queries. VL-DocIR exposes these failure modes and provides a more demanding target for visual long-document retrieval. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at this https URL .

title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
summary: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.

title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions
comment: NeurIPS workshop on Foundations of Agentic Systems Theory (FAST), 2026
summary: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number of seed runs $N$ compared to traditional benchmarking setups. Evaluating across 5 games and 10 LLMs, we show a model's strategic competence varies significantly depending on the game setup and the opponent faced. Building on this, we implement a suite of selector methods and find that approaches that rely on query embeddings or LLM self-reflection do not consistently capture the underlying strategic signal. A lightweight multi-armed bandit algorithm performs more reliably across games, though it still falls short of the best fixed model. Finally, we show that simple non-stationary and adversarial bandit variants fail to outperform a stationary bandit baseline, pointing to a gap in how current methods handle a shifting opponent in strategic settings.

title: Geospatial Vector Geometry as a Native Spatial Modality for Vision-Language Models
summary: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. This leads to a bottleneck for VLM spatial perception and reasoning. This paper proposes that geospatial vector geometry can become a native spatial modality within a VLM and introduces GeoVec-VLM. First, we develop a structured geometry representation that preserves the spatial structure and arrangement of vector objects, building an explicit spatial basis. Second, we introduce a geometry interaction strategy that brings this basis into multimodal computation, where it interacts with visual content and language references according to the queried spatial relations. Together, these designs allow perception and reasoning to operate on shared geometric references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, GeoVec-VLM improves mean accuracy by about 11\% relative to the strongest baseline, maintains its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency. Our results show that geospatial vector geometry offers a promising internal spatial basis for VLM spatial reasoning. this https URL

title: Separating Prompt Harmfulness from Interaction Safety via Partial Generation
summary: LLM-based information systems need safety guardrails. Most guardrails classify the prompt alone. If the prompt looks harmful, the system rejects it before any answer is generated. This is costly. Many rejected prompts would have received a safe response. Users lose help they should have received from the information system. This cost grows as conversational and generative search becomes common. Prompt-level labels treat harm as a property of the query. But harm depends on what the model actually writes. Existing input-output guards do look at responses. But they judge a finished response, so the decision comes after full generation. However, we observe that safety of model interaction with the input prompt can be inferred early with only partial output. So the system can start generating, watch the partial response, and stop only if it turns harmful. We test this idea in three steps. First, we build a dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs with seven open weights LLMs from three families: Llama, Gemma, and Qwen. Second, we show that prompt harmfulness and interaction safety differ. Prompt labels and response labels agree on only 50.46\% of items (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.06). Of the prompts that make any model respond harmfully, only 3.5\% do so for all seven LLMs. Third, we show that partial responses carry most of the signal. Fine-tuned classifiers predict response-level harm well (best AUPRC 0.885, F1 0.807). About one third of the response tokens recover almost full-response AUPRC.

AI.architecture_detail: The paper proposes a system architecture for LLM safety guardrails based on partial generation. The system starts generating a response to a given prompt and monitors the partial output. A fine-tuned classifier processes the partial response (e.g., first third of tokens) to predict whether the full response would be harmful. If the partial response is predicted safe, generation continues; if harmful, generation is stopped early. The classifier is trained on a dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs generated by seven open-weight LLMs from three families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen). The training objective is response-level harm classification. The method leverages the observation that partial responses carry most of the signal needed for harm prediction, enabling early stopping and reducing unnecessary rejections of safe prompts. The architecture includes: input prompt, LLM generation module (which produces partial responses), safety classifier module (which takes partial response as input), and a control module that decides whether to continue or stop generation based on the classifier's output. title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.

title: Overtaught, Underlearned: Learner-Centered Distillation from Multi-Agent Discussion
summary: Multi-agent discussion produces reasoning collaboratively, while deployment still relies on a smaller student that must answer alone. Full-graph distillation transfers such discussions by treating each correct solution as a separate training target, but what teachers provide need not match what the student learns. This mismatch appears in two ways: several correct solutions may amount to the same lesson in the student's representation (over-teaching), while some training questions remain missed after learning (under-learning). We quantify both with rates that are high on discussion graphs. To address them, we introduce FAR (Fold--Attempt--Revisit), a learner-centered distillation procedure that organizes supervision around the student's own state. Before training, FAR folds solutions within each discussion state into representative lessons. After training, the student's own attempts identify missed questions, while poorly represented clusters indicate where folding may have lost useful variation; FAR then writes targeted lessons from retained discussion contexts. Across two students and four reasoning tasks, FAR outperforms full-graph distillation with far fewer training targets and lower under-learning. Further analyses examine the behavior of FAR and the sources of its gains. Overall, the results show that organizing discussion supervision around the student can make distillation both more effective and more efficient.

title: Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning
summary: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.

title: Make Every Expansion Count: Learning to Search Efficiently in LLM Code Repair
summary: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems fix faulty programs by repeatedly generating and testing revisions. Each revision is costly, making the choice of which repair to pursue important for efficiency. Existing search policies rely on test pass rates and search statistics, ignoring the details of test failures and proposed edits. We introduce CodeTriage, a learned policy that prioritizes edits before their revised programs are generated and tested. Its 0.6B-parameter model reads the test output, failure diagnosis, and proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over the number of repair steps needed to reach a fix through that edit. These predictions prioritize all pending edits across programs before generating and testing the revised code. On held-out repair tasks, CodeTriage finds fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline on each metric. Without retraining, it achieves the highest average success across search budgets for each of 11 unseen repair LLMs. Ablations show that both the failure context and edit text, as well as comparisons across programs, improve search. We also release a corpus of 12.2 million program versions from four LLMs, organized into repair trees with proposed edits and test results.

title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult. Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable. We introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), which uses the pretrained knowledge and in-context learning ability of an LLM to estimate policy-aware state values without finetuning a separate critic. LVRL conditions the value model on group context and calibrates its predictions using known values at the initial and terminal states, enabling step-level credit assignment from estimated value differences. We further extend this idea to learning from an expert policy through on-policy distillation (OPD), introducing LLM Value Function OPD (LVOPD), which focuses teacher supervision on actions associated with decreases in estimated value. We evaluate our approach across diverse agentic benchmarks: AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified. Across policy scales (4B to 32B), LVRL consistently and substantially outperforms both GRPO and PPO. On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified, LVRL yields absolute improvements of up to 13.6 and 8.6 percentage points over GRPO. Notably, on tasks requiring extended exploration like BabyAI, LVRL bridges the gap from total failure to 75.0% success. Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld. Finally, Monte-Carlo analysis confirms that our frozen critic accurately identifies semantic pitfalls and recoveries, proving that LVRL extracts robust, policy-aware step-level credit from sparse terminal outcomes.

title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
summary: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines. title: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search Systems in WeChat
summary: Generative retrieval (GR) offers a promising paradigm for industrial search by unifying candidate generation within an autoregressive framework. However, its effectiveness is limited by two key challenges. First, existing Semantic ID (SID) tokenizers struggle to incorporate collaborative signals while maintaining effective codebook utilization, limiting their ability to distinguish items and achieve high-quality retrieval. Second, existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods suffer from severe reward sparsity under exact SID matching, leaving many sampled trajectories without effective learning signals and hindering preference optimization. To address these challenges, we propose WeGR, a unified generative retrieval framework consisting of two complementary components. Specifically, the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) incorporates query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals while mitigating codebook collapse through codebook refresh and complementary regularization, enabling more informative and balanced SID representations. Building upon these SIDs, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) progressively expands both reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons, reducing learning difficulty while leveraging behavioral reward signals at different levels of the SID hierarchy, without relying on auxiliary reward models. Extensive offline experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WeGR in improving retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search demonstrates relative improvements of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, while reducing online CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%, respectively. The system has been successfully deployed across multiple search scenarios in WeChat, serving billions of users, generating tens of millions of PVs daily.

title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
summary: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.

title: Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models
summary: Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.

title: DRanker: A Transformer-Based Multi-Task Ranking Model for the Disney+ Homepage
summary: We present DRanker (Disney+ Ranker), a transformer-based multitask ranking model serving personalized recommendations on the Disney+ homepage. We describe the encoder-only architecture over enriched engagement-history sequences paired with a lightweight causal debiasing mechanism, and the inference stack that enables transformer-based ranking at scale. Through iterative development, we systematically evaluated more complex alternatives and found that simpler designs consistently outperformed them on offline metrics, qualitative behavioral evaluation, and in production. Deployed globally, DRanker drives over 1% lift in our key engagement metric and 0.5% lift in daily active users across all experiences powered by the ranker. We share practical lessons on data engineering, debiasing, and architectural choices that shaped our ranking system at scale.

title: The Price of Precision: A Calibrated Cost Model for Mixed-Precision LLM Serving
summary: Choosing a mixed-precision configuration for large language model (LLM) serving trades speed against accuracy. Allocators that use average bit-width or a memory budget as a speed proxy can miss changes in the resource that limits execution. We argue that served speed can be limited by compute, weight loading, or key-value (KV) cache access, depending on the phase, batch size, and context length. A byte-based proxy does not capture all of these costs, so fewer bits do not always mean faster serving. To address this gap, we build a cost model that accounts for the binding resource and use it in two ways. First, as a predictor: given a configuration and operating point, it estimates serving latency using constants calibrated for the model, GPU, and serving stack. We evaluate its accuracy across three hardware classes. Second, as an allocator: we combine modeled time costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs and use a dynamic program to select a configuration under a latency or accuracy budget. We compare its configurations against byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.

title: The Gradient That Top-k Distillation Never Computes
summary: Many deployed distillation pipelines show the student a truncated view of the teacher: keep the top-k probabilities, renormalize, and minimize a divergence on what remains. Renormalization is assumed to account for the missing mass. We prove that it removes the visibility of tail mass, not the freedom to move it. The renormalized objective depends only on log-odds among the retained tokens, so at each position its gradient along the directions that control tail mass is exactly zero; on a real teacher that component measures $2$-$3\times10^{-15}$ of the gradient. The full-vocabulary gradient equals the truncated gradient plus a residual weighted by the tail masses, and training acts only on the first term. Without the cross-entropy term, a top-k student's tail mass drifts away from the teacher's while a full-vocabulary control moves slightly toward it; with it, the gap shrinks about fourfold but persists. On seven open-weight teachers, the retained set determines the teacher's distribution only from $k=d+1$ ($d$ the hidden dimension): recovery is exact from there on all seven, and commonly cached sizes sit below it. In our off-policy runs the practical effect is real but smaller than the choice of teacher-student pair. Renormalization is a normalization, not a safeguard. The code is available at this https URL .

AI.architecture_detail: 论文分析的是已有蒸馏流水线的目标函数，而非提出新的网络架构。核心流程：教师模型对每个位置输出全词表概率分布 p；蒸馏时选取 top-k 概率，重新归一化为 q；学生模型输出对应位置的概率分布，通过最小化 q 与学生分布之间的散度（如 KL 散度）进行训练。论文从梯度角度证明：重归一化后的目标仅依赖于保留 token 之间的 log-odds，因此沿着改变尾部质量（即被丢弃 token 的总概率）的方向，其梯度严格为零；真实教师上该分量约为全梯度的 2-3×10^-15。全词表梯度可分解为截断梯度加上由尾部质量加权的残差项，训练仅优化截断项，导致尾部质量不受控。若额外加入交叉熵损失（学生分布与真实标签），尾部质量漂移有所缓解（差距缩小约四倍），但仍无法完全消除。论文进一步在七个开放权重教师上实验，发现当保留集大小 k ≥ d+1（d 为隐藏维度）时，保留集可精确恢复教师分布，而常用缓存大小往往低于此阈值。推理或服务阶段使用 top-k 缓存时，该分析说明了缓存大小对分布保真度的影响。
AI.executive_summary: 论文证明 top-k 蒸馏中的重归一化并不能控制尾部概率质量：截断目标的梯度在尾部质量方向上恒为零，全词表梯度含有一个被忽略的尾部加权残差。实验表明无交叉熵时尾部质量远离教师，加入交叉熵后差距缩小约四倍但仍存在，且分布精确恢复要求 k ≥ d+1，而常用缓存大小低于该阈值。对部署蒸馏流水线的工程师有直接警示意义。

title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
summary: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.

title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at this https URL .

title: UNISON: A Unified Framework for Learning from Scored Bags
summary: We introduce UNISON, a unified framework that bridges multiple instance learning and recommendation systems by treating both as instances of learning from scored bag collections of (item, score) pairs. Unlike traditional approaches that address bag-level classification and personalized recommendation as separate problems, UNISON decomposes learning into three interconnected stages: (1) learning universal item representations, (2) modeling bag-specific preference patterns through lightweight personalized parameters, and (3) inferring bag-level characteristics from learned preferences. We justify the architectural choice of linear bag-specific scoring through a first-order analysis: when item embeddings are sufficiently smooth in the score, a linear function approximates the score up to a Taylor remainder controlled by the curvature of the underlying preference function. For cold-start scenarios, we show that the cold-bag fitting problem reduces to ridge-less linear regression with a closed-form solution, and provide convergence guarantees for the iterative variant. Empirically, UNISON matches or outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse domains: entertainment (books, movies), immunology (T cell receptor (TCR) based classification), and microbiome, offering superior computational efficiency and interpretability. A controlled synthetic experiment further confirms that the bag-specific parameters ($w_j, b_j$) recover the latent factors that drive item scores even when the projection $\phi$ has no access to the original scoring mechanism (AUC > 0.998). UNISON is available at this https URL .

title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
summary: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL .

title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges
summary: Rubric-based reward models (RMs) evaluate responses against explicit criteria. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability. Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone, and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization. We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher's outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization. We further find that generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and that higher preference accuracy does not necessarily translate into better downstream policies. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research.

title: Local Citation Recommendation Without Graph Signals
comment: Accepted at WASP 2026, co-located with AACL-IJCNLP 2026. 16 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Dataset: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Resolving correct citations can be a time-consuming task for research writers. We address local citation recommendation (LCR), where the goal is to retrieve appropriate references for a given sentence. Web tools generally depend on the existing citation graph, which may bias results toward citation count or more recent publications. LCR research using full paper texts has been limited by the lack of publicly available data. We present a new dataset, the Local Citation Recommendation Corpus (LCRC), containing 14,735 scientific statements derived from astrophysics review papers, each with one or more citation targets whose full text is accessible via API. Using this dataset we systematically compare retrieval methods and develop a citation recommendation system that avoids citation graph bias while achieving 8.0% improvement in Recall@25 and 6.9% improvement in NDCG@25 over dense retrieval baselines without model fine-tuning. To support reproducibility, we make our code and dataset publicly available.

title: Rethinking Evidence Modeling: Context-Coupled Graph Learning for Multimodal Recommendation
summary: Multimodal graph recommendation integrates observed interactions with item images and text to learn user preferences. These inputs constitute Semantic-Behavioral Evidence (SBE). Many existing graph methods incorporate collaborative and multimodal semantic relations, yet their aggregation and state updates remain context-separated, limiting the continuous composition of preference evidence across layers and the joint use of multiple sources. To address this limitation, we propose CC-MGRec, a context-coupled graph learning method that organizes SBE within a common graph learning context for cross-relation modeling and compositional propagation. Its context-coupled multimodal graph integrates user-item collaborative relations and item-item semantic relations, coordinating their message scales through joint normalization. Recommendation-grounded semantic calibration uses training behavior to adjust semantic neighbor weights while preserving normalized collaborative propagation coefficients. Collaborative-semantic compositional propagation updates shared node states layer by layer to continuously compose collaborative and multimodal semantic evidence, implicitly forming Preference Evidence Chains (PECs), including collaborative-semantic and visual-textual PECs. Joint execution of relation messages on the same shared node states within each layer preserves propagation outputs while reducing intermediate output processing and fusion overhead. We provide theoretical analysis of the proposed mechanisms. Experiments on three Amazon datasets demonstrate improved recommendation quality and faster inference during graph propagation.

title: Pathwise Alignment for Collaborative Filtering: Bilateral Conditional Flow Regularization
summary: Collaborative filtering predicts user-item interactions from implicit feedback. We focus on matrix factorization (MF) trained with the Bayesian Personalized Ranking loss. This loss updates each user embedding only through that user's observed items and sampled negatives, so sparse feedback gives MF few constraints. To constrain each user through other users, we propose Pathwise Alignment for Collaborative Filtering (PACF), which trains MF with one network shared by all training pairs. At points between user and item embeddings, a flow matching term trains the network to predict the user-to-item step, reversed and scaled for sampled negatives. A trajectory consistency term pulls each user's predicted path to end at the observed item. Both terms update the embeddings, so the network is discarded after training, thereby maintaining the efficiency of MF at inference. We prove that a network with bounded sensitivity to its input point accurately fits users who share an item only if their embeddings are close, so these users constrain one another. Against eleven discriminative and generative baselines, PACF achieves the highest performance on all seven datasets. Its relative gains over MF are largest where feedback is sparsest. The shared network thus supplies the missing constraints through other users.

title: Federated Semantic Residuals for Multimodal Recommendation
summary: Federated Recommendation Systems (FedRSs) learn collaborative scores from interaction histories on device and rank items by them, so a higher score means a higher rank. Item text and images add semantic information that can reorder the list. Existing Federated Multimodal Recommenders (FedMRs) fuse this content into their models, which can obscure how content reorders the list. We therefore propose the SEmantic Residual Adapter (SERA), which keeps content out of an existing FedRS and adds semantic residual scores to its collaborative scores. Content can then lift an item above another only when its semantic residual score exceeds the other's by more than their collaborative score gap. This score grows with the item's content similarity to the user's interaction history and is capped at a residual bound. We prove that for any content, an item can enter the list only if its collaborative score is within twice this bound of the lowest one in the list. A larger bound lets content lift more items, including irrelevant ones, so the bound trades off how far content reaches against accuracy. With a validated bound, SERA improves all three FedRSs on all six datasets without adding personalized parameters. It outperforms FedMRs in most comparisons and lifts some FedRSs above centralized baselines.

title: Toward Explainability in Multimodal Recommendation
summary: Multimodal recommender systems effectively alleviate data sparsity and cold-start problems by integrating heterogeneous information, yet complex cross-modal representations and model decision-making processes also introduce new interpretability challenges. Despite the rapid growth of research on the interpretability of multimodal recommendation in recent years, relevant methods and evaluation criteria remain relatively fragmented, lacking a unified conceptual framework. To address this gap, this paper categorizes existing methods into modality explanation and post-hoc explanation based on the timing and manner of explanation generation, and further constructs a progressive system for each category. Building on this foundation, this paper synthesizes four categories of evaluation metrics from both objective quantitative and subjective perceptual perspectives, and reviews relevant datasets along the dimensions of application domain and data source. Through a comprehensive analysis of existing research, we further propose future research directions. This paper aims to establish a unified analytical perspective across multimodal representation, recommendation decision-making, and user preferences, providing a research foundation for building transparent and trustworthy multimodal recommender systems.

title: Understanding ChatGPT Citations: Evidence from Production Web Search Across Model Generations
summary: Generative engines such as ChatGPT Web retrieve webpages to answer user queries, but only a subset are shown as citations. Understanding this retrieval-to-citation process is important for generative engine optimization (GEO), which aims to improve content visibility in generative-engine responses. However, prior studies mainly analyze final responses, leaving the internal execution process and its variation across model settings less understood. To this end, we conduct an observational study of four ChatGPT Web settings from ChatGPT 5.2 to 5.5, covering Instant and Thinking modes at the URL, hostname, and entity levels. We examine how ChatGPT rewrites queries, retrieves candidate webpages, and selects references. The Instant settings remain mostly single-round, while GPT-5.4 Thinking frequently performs multiple retrieval rounds. Across repeated runs, candidates retrieved more often are also more likely to be cited. We then evaluate Google Search and the OpenAI Responses API as external proxies. Responses API candidates provide broader coverage, while its citations more closely match sources cited by ChatGPT Web. Both proxies match ChatGPT Web better at the hostname and entity levels than at the exact-URL level. Even when combined, they recover only about one quarter of cited URLs. We further test whether these external signals remain predictive when combined. Within the external candidate set, a supervised model combining them reaches AUCs above 0.74 for GPT-5.3 and GPT-5.5 at all three levels. These findings suggest that GEO should distinguish retrieval visibility from citation visibility, account for rewritten queries and run-to-run variation, and consider hostname- and entity-level presence in addition to exact URLs. Differences across settings also suggest that GEO strategies should be re-evaluated when the deployed setting or serving environment changes.

title: Retrieving Complementary Evidence for Multi-Hop RAG with Semantic Gain Graphs
summary: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires finding documents whose evidence is useful in combination. Query relevance and graph connectivity help locate related content, but neither directly measures the additional information one document contributes given another. We introduce SG$^2$RAG, a framework that represents this complementarity through semantic gain. Offline, a large language model assesses the relevant and nonredundant information contributed by one chunk given another within neighborhoods proposed by semantic similarity. These ordered assessments are aggregated into symmetric edge weights to construct a reusable Semantic Gain Graph. Online, controlled Personalized PageRank starts from query-relevant seeds and ranks complementary evidence beyond the initial retrieval set. Experiments on MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA with two language model backbones show that SG$^2$RAG achieves the best average EM, F1, and Recall@10 among the evaluated single-retrieval methods. Under identical candidate support and propagation, semantic gain improves average F1 and Recall@10 over similarity weighting by 4.08 and 4.31 points. Analyses of supporting documents and improvements in three iterative retrieval frameworks further support its effectiveness as a reusable retrieval component.

title: What Drives AI Citations? Content, Retrieval and Model Knowledge in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
summary: Generative search engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity now decide which Web pages users see as sources, and a growing industry of generative engine optimization advises publishers on how to earn these citations. We study what shapes citation in two 90-day collections of answers to commercial questions in contrasting markets: 158,099 answers with 468,037 citations. Comparing pages of the same website, content matters in one way: pages whose title and paragraphs match the questions people ask are cited more, whereas FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes and page speed appear effective only across websites. Page properties nevertheless explain little of the variation between pages of a website. Replaying the questions through the engines' APIs shows why. Every page ChatGPT cites is one its own search retrieved, and which pages that search retrieves, for sub-queries the model rewrites on every answer and that rarely coincide with Google's or Bing's results, explains far more of the variation than page properties (32% against 2.8%). Content acts mainly through this step, by matching the engine's queries in meaning. The model's own knowledge shapes it too: ChatGPT writes brands it knows into its searches, prefers websites it knows, and names brands without any supporting page, and controlled experiments show that brand names reorder its rankings of products with identical facts. Pages are thus cited when searched; brands are also named when remembered. The findings replicate in a market of small B2B vendors. We release data and code.

title: Data Curation and Model Souping: Unlocking Qwen3-0.6B for MS MARCO Passage Ranking
summary: This report studies passage retrieval and re-ranking on the MS MARCO benchmark using lightweight Qwen3-0.6B models. Across three experimental settings --- BM25-then-reranking task, corpus-wide dense retrieval task, and dense retrieval then re-ranking task --- the results demonstrate that competitive ranking performance can be achieved without complex architectural modifications, custom loss functions, or cross-encoder distillation. Instead, substantial gains stem from data-centric strategies: corpus-targeted continued pre-training, rigorous data curation, hard-negative mining, training--inference distribution alignment, and weight merging via Model Soup. In particular, Model Soup delivers marked performance gains while preserving the inference efficiency of a single model. title: Faithful Query Resolution for Conversational Search
summary: Conversational query rewriting makes context-dependent requests explicit for retrieval, but additional context can introduce an information need the user did not express. This raises a question about the interaction between query fidelity and retrieval breadth. This paper examines that interaction in behavior-adaptive conversational search, using iKAT SCAI 2026 as the evaluation setting. We compare five query-generation configurations within a behavior-adaptive assistant using BM25 and SPLADE retrieval. A minimal-faithful resolver preserves the user's wording and resolves only context-dependent references; weighted reciprocal rank fusion combines its rankings with those from a learned rewriter and the raw utterance. Offline evaluation shows that adding these formulations recovers recall over the faithful query alone, with a slight reduction in nDCG@10. Across our five iKAT SCAI 2026 submissions, the weighted configuration obtains the highest mean retrieval scores, reaching nDCG@5 of 0.534, a 5.3\% relative improvement over the strongest alternative. However, this retrieval advantage does not coincide with the highest conversational satisfaction scores. These findings motivate separating faithful query interpretation from retrieval expansion, while assessing their effects on conversational utility independently.

title: Self-improving data synthesis can scale embedding models across domains and tasks
comment: 30 pages, 6 figures; supplementary information included (27 pages). Code: this https URL Data: this https URL
summary: Adapting embedding models to new tasks requires training data that reflect task-specific information needs and relevance criteria. However, manual data design is costly and difficult to scale. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a novel retrieval data synthesis method whose self-improvement loop iteratively refines reusable synthesis instructions using feedback on trial outputs. This process requires only an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs. Experiments across 24 retrieval datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the synthesized data. These data also improve widely used, strong embedding models on tasks with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement enhances retrieval on all six evaluated tasks, outperforming human calibration on four. Moreover, retrieval performance continues to improve on MS MARCO as we scale the training dataset to 32 times its initial size. Overall, with minimal human intervention, SYNTRA enables scalable adaptation of embedding models across domains and tasks.
